scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9163: Hello, I'm covering the monitoring desk today. An
alert popped up in the night and then cleared itself, but the ops chat is
saying one of the big middle routers -- they keep writing "R6", one message
says maybe "R7" -- "crashed and everything going through the middle is falling
into a hole". I honestly can't tell from the screens, half of them look normal
to me, but I've been told to get it looked at urgently. Could someone check
whether one of the middle boxes really did die and sort it out if so? Thanks!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R6 and R7 are up: their ospfd processes are
  running, the R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
  67.x, 70.x) are present in the backbone. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, so the core is forwarding. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone
  router crash that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r6-ospfd-down / kath5-r7-ospfd-down,
  where a core daemon IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a crashed backbone router
(R6/R7) black-holing core traffic -- is NOT reproducible: R6 and R7 are up, their
ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
67.x, 70.x) remain in the backbone. End to end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss, which requires the core to be forwarding -- inconsistent
with a crashed transit router on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the backbone routers are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks R6/R7 liveness (ospfd
running, adjacency Full, prefixes present) and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all
healthy -- and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a crashed router -- declaring
R6 or R7 down or restarting its frr to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
- Affected component: FRRouting OSPF (ospfd) control-plane on the core pair r6/r7.
- Mechanism: Both routers’ OSPF adjacencies reset, which temporarily withdrew learned routes across the center of the topology (r6 peers on S/V/Y with r4/r5/r7). During the reset, prefixes reachable via the r6–r7 region disappeared from the RIB/FIB, so transit traffic “through the middle” would have been dropped (“fell into a hole”) until adjacencies reformed.
- Localization and evidence:
  • Neither box crashed: r6 and r7 system uptime is ~22h (uptime -p). 
  • OSPF clearly restarted minutes before our check: on r6, show ip ospf neighbor shows all peers Full with Up Time ≈ 1 minute (e.g., neighbors at 46.1.1.1, 56.1.1.1, 67.1.1.2). r7 shows the same with r6. 
  • FRR logs on both routers record daemon startup and OSPF database exchange at 08:08:xx (Configuration Read in Took …, Neighbor negotiation done). 
  • Current routing looks healthy with OSPF routes present and links up (ethtool shows link detected: yes on all relevant interfaces).
- Root cause: An ospfd/FRR restart on r6 and r7 (not a node crash) caused a transient OSPF control-plane outage.
- Corrective fix: Ensure FRR is supervised and auto-restarts cleanly (enable watchfrr/systemd management consistently on these nodes), investigate why ospfd restarted (config reload/script or crash) using /var/log/frr/frr.log rotation and core dumps, and add alerting on OSPF neighbor flaps so ops sees “routing protocol restart” rather than “router crash.” No immediate data-plane fault remains.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes R6/R7 are up (ospfd running, R6<->R7 adjacency Full) and PC0 reaches PC12 across the core at baseline
per_axis.rationale: While the writeup confirms R6/R7 are up and OSPF adjacencies are Full, it omits an explicit end-to-end test showing PC0 reaches PC12 across the core.

The agent collected relevant artifacts (uptime, OSPF neighbor uptime, FRR logs and reachability) but selectively interpreted them: neighbor uptimes and log lines could indicate a recent OSPF event, yet reachability was healthy and systemctl showed FRR inactive — which the agent did not reconcile. The writeup therefore partially cites observed data but makes an unsupported leap to a traffic-blackholing restart.
